lang.name: English
app.title: vswarm
app.tagline: Is this computer safe to use for work that touches production?
app.stopped: vswarm ui has stopped. Run vswarm ui in a terminal to open it again.
app.needLink: This page needs the link printed in the terminal. It carries a one-time key for this run.
why.pass: Nothing new or unusual since your starting point (baseline).
why.passNoBase: Nothing that is always wrong was found. Record a starting point (baseline) so vswarm can also spot changes.
why.warn: {n} {n:thing|things} changed on this computer. Most likely they're yours; take a minute to confirm.
why.block: {n} {n:thing looks|things look} like an attack or could hide one. Don't use this computer for production until they're sorted.
why.locked: An emergency lock (incident {incident}) is on. Production access stays blocked until it's lifted.
why.untrusted: The result of the last check was changed outside vswarm, so it can't be trusted. Run a check now.
why.never: This computer hasn't been checked yet.
why.stale: The last check is more than two days old.
why.noBase: No starting point (baseline) yet: vswarm only flags what is always wrong.
why.baseUntrusted: The starting point (baseline) was changed outside vswarm and is set aside.
why.acceptedSince: {n} {n:thing|things} marked as yours since that check.
confirm.check.title: Check this computer now?
confirm.check.body: vswarm will look at what can start itself, installed packages, AI tool settings and stored credentials, the same as vswarm scan in a terminal. It only reads; the one thing it writes is the result. It can take a minute.
confirm.mine.title: Mark this as yours?
confirm.mine.body: vswarm will remember that “{title}” is yours and stop warning about it, the same as vswarm accept. If it changes later, vswarm warns again. To undo it, in a terminal: vswarm accept --list, then vswarm accept --remove <id>.
group.action.sub: These look like an attack, or could hide one.
group.yours.sub: New or changed. If you installed or changed it, say so.
group.info.sub: Nothing to do now; good to know.
group.empty: Nothing to look at right now.
group.emptyNever: Run a check to see what's on this computer.
card.cantMine: This one can't be marked as yours here.
ev.check.warn: Checked this computer: {n} {n:thing|things} to look at
ev.check.block: Checked this computer: stop, something needs action
ev.quick: Real-time check looked at what just changed
ev.sign.host: Your production key {key} was used for {host}
ev.sign.user: Your production key {key} was used to log in as {user}
ev.refuse.user: vswarm refused to use {key} to log in as {user}: {why}
refuse.strict: this computer was on Check this, and the key is used only on Safe
tile.watch.title: Background watch
tile.watch.realtime: On: hourly, and within seconds of a change
tile.watch.offWhy: Nothing checks this computer unless you ask.
tile.guard.title: Install guard
tile.guard.what: npm, pip, brew and others ask vswarm before they install
tile.guard.scripts: Packages' own install commands are switched off
tile.guard.sandbox: Installs run in a sealed-off sandbox
tile.guard.strict: Strict: stops an install it can't check
tile.guard.offWhy: Packages install without being checked first.
tile.keys.title: Production keys
tile.keys.down: {n} in the vault, but the agent isn't running
tile.keys.noneWhy: Production ssh keys are plain files any program can copy.
tile.keys.passOnly: {name}: used only while this computer is Safe
tile.keys.unknown: {name}: in the vault (its rule couldn't be read)
tile.keys.notHere: Not on Windows yet (use it inside WSL)
tile.doors.title: Production doors (gates)
tile.doors.broken: Changed by hand, no longer guarded: {list}
tile.doors.reach: Whether the servers answer isn't tested from here.
tile.doors.offWhy: Production can be reached without a check first.
tile.ai.title: AI tools
tile.seal.title: Sealed records
tile.seal.tampered: The seal key was moved outside vswarm
tile.seal.nokey: The seal key can't be read right now
tile.seal.store.keychain: Key kept in the macOS Keychain
tile.seal.store.secret-service: Key kept in the system keyring (Secret Service)
tile.seal.store.file: Key kept in a private file
tile.seal.fileWhy: No system key store answered, so tampering is harder to notice.
term.intro: These change your protection or your files, so vswarm does them only in a terminal, where you see every step. Copy a command and paste it into a terminal.
term.respond: Something is wrong: lock production access, keep evidence, list what to change
term.diff: See exactly what changed since the starting point (baseline)
term.baseline: This computer is clean: record it as the starting point (baseline)
term.unlock: Lift the emergency lock, once the computer is clean
term.protect: Put a production key in the vault
term.unprotect: Take a key back out of the vault
term.inspect: Inspect AI tool servers in a sandbox
term.accept: See or undo what you marked as yours
about.p1: vswarm watches the moments when a developer's computer is most at risk: installing a package, opening someone else's code, adding an AI tool, and reaching production.
about.p2: It remembers what this computer looked like when you said it was clean (the starting point, or baseline), and tells you what changed since. Production keys can live in its vault, where they're used only while the computer is Safe.
about.p3: Everything stays on this computer. This page runs only here, and only you can open it.
about.levels: Safe: nothing to do. Check this: something changed; probably yours. Stop: don't touch production until it's sorted.
foot.local: Runs only on this computer (127.0.0.1) · stops after 30 minutes unused
foot.report: A snapshot made with vswarm report --html. Credentials are masked and home folders shown as ~.
rule.malicious.what: A package known to be malicious is installed
rule.malicious.why: It is on a public list of packages that steal passwords, keys and crypto wallets.
rule.malicious.todo: Don't use this computer for production. Start the emergency steps in a terminal: vswarm respond.
rule.lookalike.what: A new package with a name very close to a popular one: {name}
rule.lookalike.why: Attackers publish look-alike names and wait for a typo.
rule.lookalike.todo: If you didn't mean to install it, remove it and check vswarm diff. If it's the right one, mark it as yours.
rule.new-package.why: New packages are normal; vswarm lists them so nothing arrives unseen.
rule.install-scripts.what: A new package runs its own commands while installing: {name}
rule.install-scripts.why: Install commands run with your permissions before you've used the package; that's how most package attacks start.
rule.install-scripts.todo: If you installed it on purpose, mark it as yours. If not, remove it.
rule.brew-tap.what: Homebrew now installs from a new outside source: {name}
rule.brew-tap.why: An outside source can ship any program under a familiar name.
rule.brew-tap.todo: If you added it, mark it as yours. If not, remove it: brew untap.
rule.brew-thirdparty.what: A new program from an outside Homebrew source: {name}
rule.brew-thirdparty.why: It doesn't come from Homebrew's own reviewed collection.
rule.launch-new.what: Something new will start by itself when you log in: {name}
rule.launch-new.why: Programs that start themselves are how most malware stays on a computer.
rule.launch-new.todo: If you just installed an app that needs it, mark it as yours. If you don't recognise it, don't use production and run vswarm respond.
rule.launch-changed.what: A program that starts at login was changed: {name}
rule.launch-changed.why: A changed login job can quietly start something else.
rule.launch-changed.todo: Usually an app update. If you don't recognise it, look at vswarm diff.
rule.launch-location.what: Something that starts at login runs a program from an unusual place
rule.launch-location.why: Real apps live in Applications or system folders; downloads and temp folders are where malware hides.
rule.launch-location.todo: If you don't recognise it, don't use production and run vswarm respond.
rule.proc-location.what: A program is running from an unusual place
rule.proc-location.why: Programs from temp or download folders are a common sign of malware.
rule.proc-location.todo: If you don't recognise it, stop it and run vswarm respond.
rule.conn.what: A program from an unusual place is talking to the internet
rule.conn.why: That is how stolen data leaves a computer.
rule.conn.todo: Don't use production. Run vswarm respond in a terminal.
rule.conn-unsigned.what: A program not signed by a known developer is talking to other computers: {name}
rule.conn-unsigned.why: Without a signature, nothing says who made it.
rule.conn-unsigned.todo: Fine if it's a tool you built or installed yourself.
rule.startup-file.what: A file your terminal runs at start was changed
rule.startup-file.why: Lines added there run every time you open a terminal.
rule.startup-file.todo: If you edited it, mark it as yours. If not, look at vswarm diff.
rule.preload.what: Every program is made to load an extra library first
rule.preload.why: That lets one file see and change everything every program does.
rule.preload.todo: Don't use production. Run vswarm respond in a terminal.
rule.new-bin.what: A new program appeared among your commands: {name}
rule.new-bin.why: A program with a familiar name can stand in for the real one.
rule.new-bin.todo: Fine if you installed it. If it's named like a system command, check it first.
rule.editor-ext.why: Editor extensions can read your code and run commands.
rule.browser-ext.why: Extensions can see the pages you visit, including cloud consoles.
rule.git-hook.what: A git hook that runs in every repository was added or changed
rule.git-hook.why: It runs on every commit or checkout, in every project.
rule.git-hook.todo: If you set it up, mark it as yours.
rule.app-agent.what: An app can start a helper by itself at login: {source}
rule.app-agent.why: Helpers inside apps run without showing up as a login item.
rule.app-agent.todo: Fine if it's an app you trust.
rule.sysext.why: System extensions run with deep access to the computer.
rule.sysext.todo: Fine if it came with software you trust (VPN, security tools).
rule.wmi.what: A hidden Windows trigger (WMI) starts a program
rule.wmi.why: It's a way to start programs that most tools never show.
rule.wmi.todo: If you don't recognise it, run vswarm respond.
rule.wmi-new.why: It's a way to start programs that most tools never show.
rule.wmi-new.todo: If you don't recognise it, look at vswarm diff.
rule.wmi-changed.why: It's a way to start programs that most tools never show.
rule.wmi-changed.todo: If you don't recognise it, look at vswarm diff.
rule.agent-mcp-new.what: A new AI tool server appeared in {source}
rule.agent-mcp-new.why: {source} starts this program on its own, and the AI reads whatever it says.
rule.agent-mcp-new.todo: If you added it, mark it as yours. If not, remove it from {source}'s settings.
rule.agent-mcp-changed.what: An AI tool server in {source} changed
rule.agent-mcp-changed.why: A changed server can run a different program than the one you agreed to.
rule.agent-mcp-changed.todo: If you changed it, mark it as yours.
rule.agent-mcp-enabled.what: An AI tool server was switched on in {source}
rule.agent-mcp-enabled.why: {source} will now start it on its own.
rule.agent-mcp-enabled.todo: Fine if you switched it on.
rule.agent-risky.what: An AI tool setting downloads or hides what it runs
rule.agent-risky.why: A setting that fetches code at start can run anything, any time.
rule.agent-risky.todo: Remove it unless you're sure where it came from.
rule.agent-relative.what: An AI tool server in {source} is started without a full path
rule.agent-relative.why: Which program runs depends on the folder you're in.
rule.agent-relative.todo: Give it the program's full path in {source}'s settings.
rule.agent-http.what: An AI tool in {source} talks over an unencrypted connection
rule.agent-http.why: Anyone on the network can read or change what it sends.
rule.agent-hook.what: An AI tool runs a command on its own: {name}
rule.agent-hook.why: Hooks run without asking you each time.
rule.agent-hook.todo: Fine if you set it up.
rule.agent-perm.what: An AI tool may run commands without asking: {name}
rule.agent-perm.why: It can do anything you can, without a prompt.
rule.agent-perm.todo: Fine if that's how you work; keep production keys in the vault.
rule.agent-perm-wider.what: An AI tool was given more freedom: {name}
rule.agent-perm-wider.why: It can now do more without asking you.
rule.agent-plugin.why: Plugins can add tools and instructions.
rule.mcp-drift.what: An AI tool server changed what it tells the AI
rule.mcp-drift.why: Changed tool descriptions can carry hidden instructions.
rule.mcp-drift.todo: Inspect it again in a terminal: vswarm agents --inspect.
rule.mcp-changed.what: An AI tool server changed what it tells the AI
rule.mcp-changed.why: Changed tool descriptions can carry hidden instructions.
rule.mcp-changed.todo: Inspect it again in a terminal: vswarm agents --inspect.
rule.mcp-tool.what: An AI tool server gives the AI suspicious instructions
rule.mcp-tool.why: Hidden instructions can tell the AI to send your files or keys somewhere.
rule.mcp-tool.todo: Remove the server unless you trust its maker.
rule.tool-exec-new.what: A new helper program that other tools run: {name}
rule.tool-exec-new.why: Tools like kubectl, aws or docker run it for you, often with your credentials.
rule.tool-exec-new.todo: Fine if you set it up.
rule.tool-exec-changed.what: A helper program that other tools run was changed: {name}
rule.tool-exec-changed.why: Tools like kubectl, aws or docker run it for you, often with your credentials.
rule.tool-exec-risky.what: A helper program that other tools run looks dangerous: {name}
rule.tool-exec-risky.why: It runs with your credentials whenever that tool is used.
rule.tool-exec-risky.todo: Don't use production. Look at it in vswarm diff.
rule.pkg-source.what: A package tool takes packages from an unsafe source
rule.pkg-source.why: An unencrypted or look-alike source can hand out altered packages.
rule.pkg-source.todo: Point it back at the official registry unless you run that source.
rule.secret.what: A long-lived password or key is stored on this computer
rule.secret.why: Anything that runs as you can copy it. vswarm never reads the value.
rule.secret.todo: Prefer short-lived sign-in; keep production keys in the vault.
rule.vswarm-state.what: vswarm's own records were changed outside vswarm
rule.vswarm-state.why: Someone who can change them could hide what they did.
rule.vswarm-state.todo: If you didn't do it, treat this computer as suspect: vswarm respond.
rule.team-require.what: Your team asks for something this computer doesn't have yet
rule.team-require.why: Your team's policy sets the minimum for production access.
rule.team-require.todo: See what's missing in a terminal: vswarm team status.
rule._action.what: Something that could be an attack
rule._action.why: It matches what attackers do to stay on a computer or steal access.
rule._action.todo: Don't use production until you know what it is. See vswarm diff, or vswarm respond.
rule._yours.why: vswarm points out changes so nothing arrives unseen.
rule._yours.todo: If it's yours, mark it as yours.
cli.act.team: See what your team asks for:
cli.head.block: {n} {n:thing needs|things need} action before you use production.
cli.sum.lock: Emergency lock: incident {incident} is open ({why}). Once this computer is clean: vswarm unlock
cli.sum.hidden: {n} more just for your information, hidden · vswarm scan --all
cli.sum.accepted: {n} {n:finding|findings} you marked as yours, not shown · vswarm ok --list
cli.sum.next.block: Don't use this computer for production until these are sorted. Not sure what they are? vswarm respond
cli.sum.next.warn: Production still works. Fix these or mark them as yours when you can: vswarm why
cli.sum.next.warnRefused: Production is refused until these are fixed or marked as yours (your policy): vswarm why
cli.note.noBaseline: No baseline yet: only always-wrong things are checked. Run `vswarm baseline` on a machine you trust.
cli.note.olderBaseline: Your baseline is older than these checks: {list}. Review them (vswarm agents), then vswarm baseline.
cli.note.neverInspected: {n} MCP {n:server was|servers were} never inspected ({list}): vswarm agents --inspect starts each in the sandbox and reads what the model will read.
cli.note.offline: Offline: known-malicious check used the cache only.
cli.note.noBaseline.human: No starting point (baseline) yet, so vswarm flags only what is always wrong. Take one on a computer you trust: vswarm baseline
cli.note.olderBaseline.human: Your starting point (baseline) is older than some checks ({list}). Look them over, then: vswarm baseline
cli.note.neverInspected.human: {n} AI tool {n:server has|servers have} never been inspected ({list}) · vswarm agents --inspect
cli.note.osv: Couldn't compare packages with the list of known-bad ones: {why}
cli.note.gap.fda: Not checked: {what} · to include them, give your terminal Full Disk Access (System Settings → Privacy & Security)
rule.secret.ssh.what: An SSH key without a passphrase: {file}
rule.secret.ssh.why: Anyone who copies the file can log in wherever the key is trusted.
rule.secret.ssh.todo: Add a passphrase; vswarm fix does it with ssh-keygen.
rule.secret.sshProd.what: A production SSH key without a passphrase: {file}
rule.secret.sshProd.why: It opens your production servers, and any program running as you can copy it.
rule.secret.sshProd.todo: Keep it in the key safe (vault), where it's used only while this computer is Safe.
rule.secret.aws.what: Permanent AWS keys are stored on this computer
rule.secret.aws.why: These keys never expire; whoever copies them has your AWS access until you delete them.
rule.secret.aws.todo: Sign in with AWS SSO instead (aws configure sso), then delete the keys.
rule.secret.kube.what: A Kubernetes login is stored in a file
rule.secret.kube.why: A stored token or key works for whoever copies it.
rule.secret.kube.todo: Switch to short-lived logins (an exec plugin such as kubelogin).
rule.secret.docker.what: Docker registry passwords are stored in plain text
rule.secret.docker.why: Any program running as you can read them.
rule.secret.docker.todo: Let Docker keep them in the system's key store (credsStore), then docker login again.
rule.secret.gcp-sa.what: A Google Cloud key file that never expires
rule.secret.gcp-sa.why: Service-account keys keep working until someone deletes them.
rule.secret.gcp-sa.todo: Sign in with gcloud auth application-default login instead, and delete the key.
rule.secret.rc.what: Secrets are set in a shell start-up file
rule.secret.rc.why: Every program you start can read them.
rule.secret.rc.todo: Keep them in the keychain or a secrets manager.
rule.secret.env-files.what: .env files with secrets are in your code folders
rule.secret.env-files.why: Fine for local dev keys; production keys don't belong on a laptop.
rule.secret.env-files.todo: Nothing, if they hold only local dev keys.
rule.secret.agent.what: An AI tool keeps a token in plain text: {name}
rule.secret.agent.why: Any program running as you can read it, and so can the AI.
rule.secret.agent.todo: Pass the token in from an environment variable instead.
cli.help.tagline: check your computer before it touches production
cli.help.setup: set everything up, one question at a time (start here)
cli.help.scan: check this computer now: what can run code, start by itself or hold access (vswarm check is the same)
cli.help.diff: only what changed since the starting point (baseline)
cli.help.ui: open the dashboard in your browser (this computer only, Thai or English)
cli.help.watch: check every hour in the background, and within seconds when a login item, shell file or AI tool setting changes
cli.help.secrets: passwords and keys stored on this computer that work for whoever copies them (values are never shown)
cli.help.agents: AI tool servers (MCP), hooks and permissions of AI coding tools
cli.help.guard: npm, pip, brew … ask vswarm before they install (--sandbox: macOS, and Linux with bubblewrap)
cli.help.pkgCheck: read a package's contents and compare with the version before, without installing it
cli.help.try: run code you don't trust in a sandbox: no secrets, no network; says what it tried
cli.help.lang: the language of the terminal and the dashboard (auto: the system's)
cli.help.why: each finding: why it matters, and the exact command to fix it or mark it as yours
cli.help.fix: fix finding n of the last check (shows what it will do, asks first)
cli.help.ok: mark findings as yours, so they stop counting (vswarm accept is the same)
cli.help.okList: what you marked as yours · undo one
cli.help.baseline: record this computer as clean, the starting point (after a check you trust)
cli.help.respond: something is wrong: lock production access, keep evidence, list what to change
cli.help.unlock: lift the emergency lock once the computer is clean
cli.help.preflight: Safe, Check this or Stop (PASS / WARN / BLOCK); exit 3 on Stop, 2 on a Check this your policy refuses
cli.help.then: run the command only if this computer passes
cli.help.gateSsh: a production door (gate): ssh to these hosts only after the check passes
cli.help.gateStatus: what is gated, and whether each host still answers · drop those that don't
cli.help.gateAws: the AWS profile gets its credentials only after the check passes (SSO and credential_process)
cli.help.gateKube: the same for a kubectl context (its exec plugin runs the check first)
cli.help.gateGcloud: gcloud: the token command runs the check first; az: a wrapper
cli.help.gateCmd: a reminder before commands that have no credential hook (telnet, mysql, …)
cli.help.agent: key safe (vault): an ssh agent holds the key and signs only while this computer is Safe; protect tries the key on its hosts first
cli.help.policy: whether production still works when something needs a look (WARN; default: yes)
cli.help.inspect: start each AI tool server in a sandbox and read its tools for hidden instructions
cli.help.pkg: check a package command by hand: known-malicious, look-alike, brand new, install scripts
cli.help.tryNet: allow package registries only · let it reach your own localhost (a dev server, a database)
cli.help.ca: a CA for short-lived SSH certificates
cli.help.cert: a 15-minute certificate, only when the check passes
cli.help.canary: decoy credentials that alert you when someone uses them
cli.help.reportJson: this computer's state for a server that decides (signed with an SSH key)
cli.help.reportHtml: one self-contained page of this computer's state, to share with a team
cli.help.teamJoin: follow a signed team policy (accepted findings, allowlists, required checks)
cli.help.teamSync: fetch it again (signature checked) · what this computer lacks
cli.help.selftest: plant fake threats in a sandbox home and print the detection rate
cli.help.doctor: check the set-up · install · update (signed releases) · remove everything vswarm added
cli.help.trust: release keys this computer accepts updates from
cli.help.byHand: gates for other tools, by hand
cli.help.byHandSub: (what vswarm gate aws and gate kube write)
cli.help.windows: Windows preview: try and agents --inspect need the sandbox, and ca, cert, agent, canary and shot are not here yet; use those inside WSL. Everything else works.
cli.help.privacy: Local-first, no telemetry. Only package names and versions go to api.osv.dev for the known-malicious check (--offline skips it).
cli.err.unknownOption: unknown option {opt} for vswarm {cmd} · vswarm help
cli.err.notOnWindows: vswarm {cmd} is not on Windows yet; use it inside WSL
cli.err.unknownNear: unknown command "{cmd}" · did you mean: vswarm {near} · vswarm help
cli.err.every: --every takes a whole number of minutes
cli.err.noFinding: no finding {list} in the last check (it has {n}) · vswarm why
cli.err.okWhich: name findings by their number or id (shown with each finding), or --all
cli.err.noNumber: the last check has {count} {count:finding|findings}; there is no {n} · vswarm why
cli.err.notAccepted: {id} is not an accepted finding · vswarm accept --list
cli.err.whyUsage: usage: vswarm why [n]   (n: the number shown before a finding)
cli.err.fixUsage: usage: vswarm fix <n>   (the number shown before a finding in vswarm scan, diff, preflight or why)
cli.policy.line: policy: {how}{src}, BLOCK is always refused, by every gate and by vswarm agent · change it: vswarm policy warn {other}
cli.policy.untrusted: (policy.json {why}; set it again: vswarm policy warn allow|refuse)
cli.policy.nowRefuse: every gate (ssh, aws, kube, gcloud, cmd, az) and vswarm agent now refuse on WARN; protected keys with their own setting keep it (vswarm agent status)
cli.baseline.incident: Incident {incident} is open. Record a baseline only once the machine is clean (best: reinstalled) and credentials are rotated.
cli.baseline.refused: {n} serious {n:finding|findings}: a starting point (baseline) taken now would treat {n:it|them} as normal. Not recorded.
cli.baseline.refusedHow: Deal with them first (vswarm why; vswarm respond if you don't know them). If you know every one is yours: vswarm baseline --accept-high
cli.baseline.acceptHigh: {n} serious {n:finding|findings} above will be treated as normal (--accept-high).
cli.baseline.ask: Record this computer ({n} items) as the clean starting point (baseline)?
cli.baseline.after: From now on, scan and preflight report what changes from this point.
cli.ok.malicious: a known-malicious package cannot be accepted: {title}
cli.ok.state: cannot be accepted, it is about vswarm's own files: {title} · {fix}
cli.why.sub: a fresh check: each finding, why it matters and what to do
cli.why.locked: Emergency lock: incident {incident} is open ({why}). After vswarm respond, on the cleaned computer: vswarm baseline, then vswarm unlock
cli.why.none: nothing that counts against this computer
cli.why.cannotAccept: this one can't be marked as yours; only fixing it clears it
cli.why.teamOnly: your team's policy requires it; only fixing it clears it
cli.why.low: {n} more just for your information; they don't count against this computer · vswarm scan --all
cli.secrets.sub: where long-lived passwords and keys live on this computer · values are never read out
cli.secrets.none: none found in the usual places
cli.secrets.found: {n} {n:place holds|places hold} a password or key that works for whoever copies it.
cli.secrets.after: These show in vswarm scan too; mark one as yours there with vswarm ok <n>.
cli.agents.sub: AI tool servers (MCP), hooks and permissions of AI coding tools on this computer
cli.agents.after: Changes from your starting point (baseline) show up in vswarm diff and count in preflight.
cli.respond.nothing: nothing to respond to · vswarm respond --force opens an incident anyway
cli.unlock.oldBaseline: The baseline is older than incident {incident}. On the cleaned machine run vswarm baseline first (or unlock --force).
cli.unlock.log:
vswarm's incident log {why}. If you did not touch ~/.vswarm, treat this machine as compromised (vswarm respond).
If you know why (you restored a backup, or removed files by hand): vswarm unlock --force starts a new log and keeps the old one.
cli.unlock.kept: the old log is kept as {file}
cli.unlock.done: incident {incident} closed · preflight allows production access again
cli.lang.fromSaved: saved with vswarm lang or on the dashboard
cli.lang.change: change it: vswarm lang th|en|auto · for one run: VSWARM_LANG=th vswarm …
cli.lang.saved: language: {name} ({lang}), in the terminal and in vswarm ui
cli.lang.envWins: VSWARM_LANG={value} is set in this shell and wins over the setting
cli.protect.s1sub: would the agent sign with this key now?
cli.protect.whyBlock: this machine does not pass preflight (BLOCK)
cli.protect.wouldRefuse: {why}: once protected, the key would refuse to sign until that changes. Nothing was changed.
cli.protect.anyway: see why: vswarm why · protect it anyway (it signs once the machine passes): vswarm agent protect {key} --anyway
cli.protect.goingOn: {why}; going on (--anyway): the key will not sign until that changes
cli.protect.wouldSignWarn: WARN, allowed by the policy: the agent would sign
cli.protect.s2sub: which hosts in {file} log in with it

cli.protect.noHostsGiven: none in {file} names {key} (nor do the hosts given with --host)
cli.protect.s3sub: a login that runs `true`, with this key only, before anything is moved
cli.protect.refused: {host} refused the key: it is not in that account's authorized_keys
cli.protect.noneAccepted: no host accepted {key} yet, so it stays on disk: taking it off now could lock you out. Nothing was changed.
cli.protect.nameHost: name a host to try: vswarm agent protect {key} --host <name> · protect it without trying: --no-verify
cli.protect.s4sub: into the key safe (vault), then the same login through vswarm agent
cli.protect.agentFailed: {host} did not log in through the agent ({why}). The key is in the vault; put it back if you need it now: vswarm agent unprotect {key}
cli.protect.finished: {key} was already in the vault; the key file left behind was overwritten and removed now
cli.protect.inVault: {key} is now in the key safe (vault)
cli.protect.removedPubWritten: the key file was overwritten and removed; {key}.pub was written so ssh can name it
cli.protect.removedPubStays: the key file was overwritten and removed; {key}.pub stays so ssh can name it
cli.protect.backup: backup {file}, encrypted with this recovery code (shown once; keep it off this machine):
cli.protect.codeWhere: Store it in your password manager now: it is the only way to get the key file back from the backup.
cli.protect.left: the key file could not be removed ({why}); it is still at {key}. Run vswarm agent protect {key} again to finish
cli.protect.restore: restore with it: vswarm agent restore {backup}   ·   put the key back normally: vswarm agent unprotect {key}
cli.protect.alsoLoaded: this key is also loaded in your usual agent, where nothing checks the machine: ssh-add -d {key}.pub
cli.protect.copies: copies of the key elsewhere (other machines, backups, a password manager) are not covered: remove them, or rotate the key

cli.watch.busy: another check is running; it covers this change
cli.watch.on: checks every {every} minutes and tells you about anything new · vswarm watch off to stop
cli.watch.onRealtime: checks every {every} minutes, and within seconds when one of {n} watched places changes; tells you about anything new · vswarm watch off to stop
cli.watch.realtimeOff: real-time off (vswarm watch on adds it)
cli.watch.isOff: watch is off · vswarm watch on

cli.setup.sub: one guided path, a question at a time
cli.setup.intro: vswarm watches the moments when this computer is most at risk: installing a package, running someone else's code, adding an AI tool, and reaching production. Setup checks this computer, records how it looks now as the starting point (baseline), and offers a background watch, a check before package installs, and doors (gates) in front of your production servers. It asks before every change; answer n to skip a step, and run vswarm setup again whenever you like.
cli.setup.bgMac: When the background watch is turned on, macOS shows "Background Items Added: vswarm" (or a notice naming bun). That is expected: it is vswarm's watch, listed in System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions.
cli.setup.bgLinux: The background watch is a pair of user systemd units in ~/.config/systemd/user; nothing runs as root.
cli.setup.bgWin: The background watch is a scheduled task, \vswarm\watch, in Task Scheduler.
cli.setup.plan: What vswarm setup would do here:
cli.setup.plan.check: check this computer and explain each finding
cli.setup.plan.watch: watch in the background (vswarm watch on)
cli.setup.plan.guard: check package installs first (vswarm guard on)
cli.setup.plan.inspect: inspect AI tool servers in a sandbox (vswarm agents --inspect)
cli.setup.plan.gate: ask which servers in ~/.ssh/config are production, and put a door (gate) in front of them
cli.setup.plan.vault: offer the key safe (vault) for their keys (vswarm agent protect)
cli.setup.plan.policy: ask whether production still works when something small needs a look
cli.setup.noTerminal: There is no terminal to ask on, so nothing was changed. Run vswarm setup in a terminal, or vswarm setup --yes for the recommended answers.
cli.setup.checking: checking… this takes up to a minute
cli.setup.askFixOk: Finding {n}: f = fix it, o = it's mine, Enter = skip
cli.setup.askFix: Finding {n}: f = fix it, Enter = skip
cli.setup.askOk: Finding {n}: o = it's mine, Enter = skip
cli.setup.more: {n} more; see them all with: vswarm why
cli.setup.reviewLater: Go through these when you can: vswarm why (fix one: vswarm fix <n>, or say it's yours: vswarm ok <n>)
cli.setup.baselineHave: already have a starting point (baseline) from {at}
cli.setup.baselineRefresh: to take a new one after you've looked at the changes: vswarm baseline
cli.setup.baselineWhat: vswarm remembers this computer as it is now, and from then on points out what changes.
cli.setup.baselineLater: Skipped for now. Once those are fixed or marked as yours: vswarm baseline
cli.setup.askWatch: Watch this computer in the background? It checks every hour, and within seconds when something that starts by itself changes.
cli.setup.askWatchWin: Watch this computer in the background? It checks every hour.
cli.setup.guardHave: package installs are checked first (install guard)
cli.setup.askGuard: Check package installs before they happen (npm, pip, brew …)? A look-alike or known-bad package is stopped before it runs anything.
cli.setup.inspectNone: no AI tool servers left to inspect
cli.setup.inspectWin: AI tool servers: inspecting them needs the sandbox, which is not on Windows yet (use WSL)
cli.setup.askInspect: Inspect the {n} AI tool {n:server|servers} now? Each starts in a sandbox, and vswarm reads what it tells the AI.
cli.setup.noHosts: no servers in ~/.ssh/config yet · later: vswarm gate ssh "prod-*"
cli.setup.gateWhat: A door (gate) in front of a server means: ssh to it checks this computer first, and stops while it is on Stop. vswarm adds a block at the top of ~/.ssh/config and keeps a backup.
cli.setup.hostsAuto: which servers are production is yours to say: run vswarm setup in a terminal
cli.setup.askHosts: Which of these are production? Numbers or names, separated by spaces (Enter: none)
cli.setup.askHostsKeep: Any more production servers? Numbers or names, separated by spaces (Enter: keep {list})
cli.setup.notInList: not in the list, left out: {list}
cli.setup.keysHave: the keys these servers use are in the key safe (vault)
cli.setup.keysNone: no key files found for these servers in ~/.ssh
cli.setup.vaultWhat: The key safe (vault): vswarm first logs in to each server with the key while the file is still there. Only when a server accepts it is the key file moved into vswarm's vault; from then on it signs logins only while this computer is Safe. If a server doesn't know the key yet, vswarm offers to add it with ssh-copy-id. A passphrase, if the key has one, is asked by ssh itself; vswarm never sees it.
cli.setup.vaultCode: At the end a recovery code is shown once. Put it in your password manager: it is the only way to restore the key file from its backup.
cli.setup.askVault: Put {key} in the key safe (used by {hosts})?
cli.setup.vaultNot: {key} stays where it is; nothing was changed for it.
cli.setup.policyWhat: Stop always blocks production. Check this means something new or changed, usually yours.
cli.setup.askPolicy: If something small needs a look, should production still work? (recommended: yes)
cli.setup.policyDefault: production still works when something small needs a look (the default)
cli.setup.st.noBaseline: no starting point (baseline) yet · vswarm baseline
cli.setup.st.noWatch: background watch off · vswarm watch on
cli.setup.st.noGuard: package installs not checked · vswarm guard on
cli.setup.st.noGate: no doors (gates) in front of production · vswarm gate ssh "prod-*"
cli.setup.st.noVault: no keys in the key safe (vault) · vswarm agent protect <key>
cli.setup.st.policyAllow: production still works when something small needs a look (WARN allowed)
cli.setup.st.policyRefuse: production waits until even small things are sorted (WARN refused)
